meta.title: Why Rhythm Playing Lives Up Here
meta.summary: Three concrete reasons strings 1-2-3 carry so much rhythm playing, plus a climb-the-set practice routine using the metronome and the chord detector.

spans.text: Strings 1-2-3 aren't what's left over when you can't manage a full six-string chord. A lot of rhythm playing lives up here on purpose, for three concrete reasons.

items.text: Strings 1-2-3 sit above the bass and above most vocal melodies, so a triad up there doesn't fight either one for space.
Three fingers, no barre, no thumb wrapped over the neck — nothing to set up before the next chord.
Changing chords means sliding a couple of frets, not jumping the width of the neck.

spans.text: None of the three is a consolation prize. Together they're why a rhythm part reaches for this set on purpose, not by default.

Strings 1-2-3 are one set of four. Chapter 2 takes the other three — strings 2-3-4, 3-4-5, and 4-5-6 — and works out why their grips aren't identical to these, even for the exact same chord. Same terminology, same three inversions — just three more places for them to live.
